questions.ref: Module 21 · Exemplar 21.B Pressure Injuries · Pathophysiology & Risk Factors
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.stem: An 83-year-old client with Parkinson disease and moderate dementia is admitted with aspiration pneumonia. The Braden scale total is 9. The nurse reviews the admission data. Which findings contribute to the client's risk for pressure injury? Select all that apply.
options: Temperature 38.7 °C (101.7 °F)
Serum albumin 2.8 g/dL and total lymphocyte count 1,100/mm³
Radial and pedal pulses 2+ bilaterally
Slides toward the foot of the bed when the head of the bed is raised
Wears bilateral hearing aids that correct a hearing loss
Oriented to self only; grimaces with turning but cannot say where it hurts
optionRationales: Correct. Fever raises the metabolic rate and oxygen demand, so tissue compressed over a bony prominence becomes ischemic faster.
Correct. Albumin below 3.5 g/dL and a low lymphocyte count are the nutrition markers the slides say to monitor; poor protein status means less padding and poor tissue repair.
Incorrect. Palpable 2+ pulses show adequate arterial flow to the extremities; this is not a risk factor.
Correct. Sliding down with the head of the bed raised creates shear: the skin sticks to the sheet while the skeleton slides, tearing deep vessels over the sacrum.
Incorrect. A corrected hearing loss does not change the client's ability to feel or respond to pressure.
Correct. Decreased mental status means the client cannot recognize or report pressure-related discomfort or reposition in response to it.
questions.rationale: A Braden total of 9 is very high risk, and the individual cues explain why. Fever (excess body heat) raises oxygen demand, low albumin and lymphocytes reflect inadequate nutrition, sliding in bed produces shear, and confusion limits the client's ability to sense and respond to pressure. Normal pulses and corrected hearing do not raise risk. Connecting lab values and vital signs to the risk factors lets the nurse target each one in the plan of care.
questions.takeaway: Translate every cue — vital sign, lab, behavior — into a pressure-injury risk factor before planning care.
questions.hintContent: Recall the slide risk factors (immobility, nutrition, moisture, mental status, sensation, heat, age, chronic illness, shear) and which labs the slides use to monitor nutrition.
questions.hintStrategy: Test each option on its own: does this finding reduce tissue tolerance, add shear, or impair the client's ability to feel or move? If not, leave it unselected.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Exemplar 21.B Pressure Injuries · Four Stages of Pressure Injuries
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.stem: An 83-year-old client on bed rest for pneumonia has a 2 × 2 cm area of intact, nonblanchable redness over the right heel that feels spongy on palpation. The left heel has an intact 1 × 1 cm blister filled with clear fluid. Both heels are resting directly on the mattress. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Document both heel findings as reactive redness and recheck them at the next turn
Open the left heel blister with a sterile needle so the fluid can drain
Float both heels off the mattress with pillows placed lengthwise under the calves
Massage the right heel gently to restore circulation to the boggy tissue
optionRationales: Incorrect. Reactive redness blanches and fades; nonblanchable redness is a Stage 1 injury and a clear-fluid blister is Stage 2. Neither is normal.
Incorrect. A clear-fluid blister is a Stage 2 injury; opening it creates an open wound and infection risk and does not remove the cause.
Correct. The right heel is Stage 1 and the left is Stage 2. Both were caused by unrelieved pressure, so offloading the heels is the immediate priority to prevent progression.
Incorrect. Massage over reddened bony prominences damages fragile capillaries and worsens deep tissue injury.
questions.rationale: Staging comes first: intact nonblanchable redness with bogginess is Stage 1, and an intact clear-fluid blister is Stage 2. Both injuries share a cause, which is the heels resting on the mattress. The first action is to remove that pressure by floating the heels. Documentation, wound care, and care-plan changes follow. Massage and opening the blister cause more harm.
questions.takeaway: Stage it, then remove the cause: heels with Stage 1 or 2 injuries get floated off the bed right away.
questions.hintContent: Recall what nonblanchable redness and a clear-fluid blister mean for staging, and what caused both injuries in this client.
questions.hintStrategy: First decide the stage of each heel, then ask which option stops the process that is still happening. Rule out any option that adds trauma.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Exemplar 21.B Pressure Injuries · Pathophysiology & Risk Factors
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.stem: A client's Braden subscale scores are sensory perception 2, moisture 2, activity 1, mobility 2, nutrition 1, and friction & shear 1. Over the left ischial tuberosity there is a 1.5 × 1 cm shallow, open area with a pink, moist bed and no slough or visible fat. Which statement by the nurse identifies the priority problems for the plan of care?
options: “The total of 13 is moderate risk, and the ischial area is a Stage 1 injury, so the focus is potential for impaired skin integrity.”
“The total of 9 is very high risk; the ischial area is a Stage 2 open wound, so impaired skin integrity and infection risk apply.”
“The total of 9 is mild risk, and the ischial area is a Stage 2 open wound, so the focus is situational low self-esteem.”
“The total of 9 is very high risk, but the ischial area is Stage 3, so the focus is potential for impaired skin integrity.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. The subscales total 9, not 13, and an open wound is not Stage 1. Potential for impaired skin integrity applies only when the skin is still intact.

Correct. The subscales total 9 (very high risk). A shallow, pink, moist open area is partial-thickness loss (Stage 2). An actual wound means impaired skin integrity, and a broken barrier adds risk for infection.
Incorrect. On the Braden scale, a low score means high risk, so 9 is not mild risk. Low self-esteem is not the physiologic priority here.
Incorrect. No fat is visible, so the wound is not Stage 3. And because the skin is already open, the problem is actual impaired skin integrity, not potential.
questions.rationale: This item combines three skills. First, the six subscales total 9, and because the Braden scale is inverse, 9 is very high risk. Second, a shallow, pink, moist open area without fat is a Stage 2 (partial-thickness) injury. Third, once injury exists, the diagnosis changes from potential to actual impaired skin integrity, and an open barrier adds risk for infection. These actual physiologic problems take priority over psychosocial diagnoses.
questions.takeaway: Low Braden = high risk; open skin = actual impaired skin integrity + risk for infection.
questions.hintContent: Recall the Braden range and its direction, the depth of tissue loss in each stage, and when the slide diagnoses change from potential to actual.
questions.hintStrategy: Add the subscales yourself, stage the wound from its description, then pick the option in which all three parts are correct. Any single wrong part eliminates an option.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Exemplar 21.B Pressure Injuries · Prevention
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.stem: An 81-year-old client with dysphagia after a stroke receives a pureed diet with an order for the head of the bed at 30° or higher during meals and for 1 hour afterward. The client is incontinent, has a Stage 1 sacral pressure injury, eats about 30% of meals, and has a serum albumin of 2.9 g/dL. Which interventions should the nurse include in the plan of care? Select all that apply.
options: Keep the head of the bed at 30° with the knee gatch slightly raised during and after meals
Massage the reddened sacral area at each turn to bring blood back to the tissue
Cleanse with a mild cleanser, pat dry, and apply a barrier cream after each incontinent episode
Turn the client to a 90° side-lying position to keep all weight off the sacrum
Offer a high-protein supplement between meals and trend weight and albumin
Float the heels with pillows placed lengthwise under the calves
optionRationales: Correct. Thirty degrees meets the aspiration-prevention order while limiting sacral shear; raising the knee gatch keeps the client from sliding down.
Incorrect. Massage over reddened bony prominences breaks fragile capillaries and worsens deep damage.
Correct. Urine and stool bring moisture and enzymes that macerate skin; gentle cleansing and a barrier product protect it.
Incorrect. A 90° side-lying position loads the greater trochanter; a 30° lateral tilt with pillows takes weight off the sacrum and the hip.
Correct. Poor intake and low albumin show nutritional compromise; supplements and trending nutrition markers support skin integrity.
Correct. The heels are high-risk prominences in a bed-bound client; floating them offloads pressure.
questions.rationale: This plan must balance competing needs. The dysphagia order requires the head of the bed at 30° or higher, and the slides call for 30° or lower to reduce shear, so 30° with the knee gatch meets both. Each remaining intervention targets one of the client's risk factors: moisture (barrier cream), poor nutrition (supplements, trending albumin), and pressure on the heels (floating). Massage and 90° side-lying cause harm.
questions.takeaway: Aspiration risk and shear meet at 30° with the knee gatch; then target each risk factor the client has.
questions.hintContent: Recall the HOB rule for shear, the positioning angle that spares the hip, and how moisture and low albumin raise risk.
questions.hintStrategy: Match each option to one of the client's cues (dysphagia, incontinence, Stage 1 sacrum, low intake). Keep options that fix a cue safely; drop those that add pressure or trauma.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Exemplar 21.B Pressure Injuries · Prevention
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort
questions.stem: A client with pneumonia and a Stage 1 sacral pressure injury finished breakfast at 0800 and has an order to keep the head of the bed at 30° or higher for 1 hour after meals. At 1030 the nurse finds the head of the bed at 60° and the client slid down toward the foot of the bed. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Keep the head of the bed at 60° until lunch to prevent any aspiration
Ask the UAP to pull the client up in bed by the arms after lunch
Apply cornstarch to the sacrum to reduce friction against the sheets
Lift the client with a draw sheet and two staff; set the HOB at 30°
optionRationales: Incorrect. The 1-hour post-meal window has passed; keeping the HOB at 60° continues the shear that is damaging the sacrum.
Incorrect. Pulling by the arms drags the skin across the sheet (friction and shear), and delaying leaves the client sliding.
Incorrect. Cornstarch clumps when wet and irritates the skin; it is on the slides' avoid list and does not fix shear.
Correct. Sliding with the HOB high causes sacral shear over an existing Stage 1 injury. Lifting with a draw sheet avoids friction, and 30° meets the post-meal order while reducing shear.
questions.rationale: A client sliding down a bed raised to 60° has shear: the sacral skin stays fixed to the sheet while the skeleton slides, tearing deep vessels under an area that is already injured. The aspiration-prevention window ended at 0900, so the nurse lifts the client with a draw sheet and a second staff member and lowers the HOB to 30°. Dragging and powders add damage.
questions.takeaway: Sliding + high HOB = shear: lift (never drag) and bring the HOB to ≤ 30° once aspiration precautions allow.
questions.hintContent: Recall what happens to deep sacral tissue when the HOB is high and the client slides, and how long the post-meal HOB order applies.
questions.hintStrategy: Check the times in the stem first to see whether the aspiration order still applies. Then choose the action that removes the damaging force without adding friction.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Exemplar 21.B Pressure Injuries · Nursing Process
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.stem: On day 7 of a pressure-injury plan of care, the nurse evaluates an older adult who on admission had nonblanchable sacral redness, a clear-fluid blister on the left heel, a shallow pink open area on the left ischium, and a serum albumin of 2.8 g/dL. Which finding requires the nurse to revise the plan of care?
options: Sacral redness now blanches and fades within 30 minutes of turning
Left heel blister has reabsorbed; the skin is intact and the heel is floated
Left ischial wound is now 0.4 cm deep with yellow fat visible in the base
Eats 75% of meals plus two supplements; albumin has risen to 3.6 g/dL
optionRationales: Incorrect. Redness that now blanches and fades shows the Stage 1 sacral injury is resolving; the plan is working here.
Incorrect. A reabsorbed blister with intact skin shows the Stage 2 heel injury is healing.

Correct. The ischial wound has progressed from Stage 2 (partial thickness) to Stage 3 (fat visible). The injury is worsening, so positioning, seating, and the support surface must be reassessed and the plan revised.
Incorrect. Better intake and an albumin now in the normal range (at least 3.5 g/dL) show the nutrition goals are being met.
questions.rationale: Evaluation compares current findings with the baseline. Three findings show progress: blanching sacral redness, a healed heel, and better intake with a rising albumin. The ischial wound now shows fat, so it has moved from Stage 2 to Stage 3. A wound that is deepening means the plan is not working for that site, so the nurse reassesses pressure relief there and revises the plan.
questions.takeaway: A wound that moves up a stage during treatment means the plan has failed at that site — reassess and revise.
questions.hintContent: Recall the tissue depth that defines each stage and the labs used to evaluate nutrition.
questions.hintStrategy: For each option, compare it with the admission finding and ask: better, same, or worse? Revise the plan for the finding that is worse.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Exemplar 21.B Pressure Injuries · RYB Wound Care & Debridement
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation

tabs.title: Nurses' Notes
tabs.html: 1400: 58-year-old client with T10 paraplegia and type 2 diabetes admitted from home with a known Stage 3 right ischial pressure injury. Wound 5 × 4 × 1.5 cm; moderate thick green drainage with a foul odor after cleansing. Periwound skin red, warm, and indurated, with redness extending 3 cm from the wound edge (outlined with a skin marker). Client reports increased pain at the wound and feeling ‘achy and hot.’ Uses a foam wheelchair cushion that is 6 years old.

tabs.title: Orders
tabs.html:
• Wound culture now
  • IV antibiotic as prescribed — start after the culture is obtained
  • Bed rest on low-air-loss mattress; no sitting
  • Wound care nurse and dietitian consults

questions.stem: Refer to the Nurses' Notes, Vital Signs, Laboratory Results, and Orders. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Obtain the wound culture as prescribed
Administer the first dose of the prescribed IV antibiotic
Arrange for a replacement pressure-redistribution cushion for the client's wheelchair
Massage the indurated skin around the wound to improve local blood flow
optionRationales: Correct. The findings indicate an infected pressure injury. The culture is collected before the first antibiotic dose so the results accurately identify the organism.
Incorrect. The antibiotic is given promptly, but only after the culture is obtained, as ordered.
Incorrect. The old cushion should be addressed before discharge, but the client is on bed rest with no sitting; treating the infection comes first.
Incorrect. Massaging inflamed tissue causes further damage.
questions.rationale: The cue cluster points to an infected Stage 3 pressure injury: increased pain, purulent foul-smelling drainage, spreading warm redness, fever, and a WBC of 15,800/mm³. High glucose and low albumin also slow healing. The culture must be collected before the first antibiotic dose so the results identify the organism accurately; then the antibiotic is given without delay. The nurse evaluates response by trending temperature, WBC, and the marked border of redness, while pressure relief continues.
questions.takeaway: Infected pressure injury: culture first, then the antibiotic — and keep pressure off the wound.
questions.hintContent: Recall the signs of an infected wound, why culture timing matters when antibiotics are ordered, and how glucose and albumin affect healing.
questions.hintStrategy: Name the problem from the cue cluster first. Then look at the Orders tab and ask which prescribed action has to happen before another can be done correctly.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Exemplar 21.B Pressure Injuries · Four Stages of Pressure Injuries
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential

tabs.title: Nurses' Notes
tabs.html: 1000: 81-year-old client, day 2 after surgical repair of a hip fracture. Confused at night; on bed rest. Incontinent of urine; linens found damp. Eating about 30% of meals. Night-shift report states the client has been lying on the back since 0600 because the client "fights turning." Sacrum: 3 × 3 cm area of redness, skin intact; redness does not blanch and has not faded 30 minutes after the client was turned to the side; warmer than surrounding skin. Heels pink and blanchable. Braden score 11.

questions.stem: Refer to the Nurses' Notes and Vital Signs. The nurse determines that the client has a Stage 1 pressure injury of the sacrum. Which actions should the nurse include in the client's care? Select all that apply.
options: Massage the sacral area to restore blood flow
Reposition off the sacrum at least every 2 hours using a draw sheet
Place a doughnut cushion under the sacrum
Cleanse with a mild cleanser, pat dry, and apply a barrier cream after each incontinent episode
Raise the head of the bed to 60° for comfort
Assess the sacral skin color and blanch response at each turn
optionRationales: Incorrect. Massage over reddened bony prominences damages tissue further.
Correct. Pressure relief is the priority; reposition at least every 2 hours and lift with a draw sheet to avoid shear.
Incorrect. Doughnut devices reduce blood flow to surrounding tissue.
Correct. Managing moisture from incontinence protects the skin from maceration.
Incorrect. HOB above 30° increases shear on the sacrum.
Correct. Return of blanching and fading redness show the injury is resolving; open skin would show progression.
questions.rationale: Nonblanchable redness on intact sacral skin that has not faded 30 minutes after turning is a Stage 1 pressure injury. The notes explain why it formed: hours on the back, damp linens, poor intake, and confusion. Correct care addresses those causes. The nurse repositions off the sacrum at least every 2 hours with a draw sheet, manages moisture with gentle cleansing and a barrier cream, and rechecks the blanch response at each turn. Massage, doughnut devices, and a HOB above 30° all worsen tissue damage.
questions.takeaway: Stage 1: get off it, keep it dry, recheck the blanch response.
questions.hintContent: Recall what defines Stage 1 and which prevention measures address pressure, moisture, and shear.
questions.hintStrategy: Link each option to a risk factor in the notes. Keep options that remove pressure, moisture, or shear or that monitor the injury; eliminate anything the slides say to avoid.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Exemplar 21.B Pressure Injuries · Four Stages of Pressure Injuries
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a 58-year-old client with darkly pigmented skin who has been on bed rest for 4 days after a stroke. The skin was assessed in natural light. Which findings suggest a pressure injury is developing? Select all that apply.
options: Dry, flaky skin on both shins
A 4 × 3 cm area over the left greater trochanter that is darker and more purplish than the surrounding skin
The same area is warmer to the touch than adjacent skin
Capillary refill in the fingers is 2 seconds
The same area is firm and indurated on palpation
The client reports tenderness when the area is touched
optionRationales: Incorrect. Dry, flaky shins reflect xerosis and need moisturizing, but they are not a pressure injury.
Correct. In dark skin, erythema may not be visible; a localized darker, purple, or bluish area over a bony prominence is a key sign.
Correct. Localized warmth reflects inflammation beneath the skin.
Incorrect. Capillary refill of 2 seconds is normal peripheral perfusion.
Correct. Induration or firmness (or bogginess) signals tissue damage under intact skin.
Correct. Localized pain or tenderness over a pressure point often precedes visible change.
questions.rationale: In darkly pigmented skin, Stage 1 may show as darkening or a purplish or bluish tone instead of redness, and blanching can be hard to see. The nurse therefore uses the assessment techniques from the skin-assessment and nursing-process lessons: inspect in good light and palpate. Compared with nearby skin, the area may be warmer or cooler, firm or boggy, and tender. Dry shins and a normal finger capillary refill are not signs of pressure injury.
questions.takeaway: Dark skin: look for darkening, then confirm Stage 1 by touch — temperature, firmness, and pain.
questions.hintContent: Recall how Stage 1 appears in people of color and what palpation adds to inspection over a bony prominence.
questions.hintStrategy: Focus on findings located over the bony prominence and compared with the surrounding skin. General skin findings elsewhere do not help stage this area.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Exemplar 21.B Pressure Injuries · Prevention
questions.clientNeed: Health Promotion and Maintenance
questions.stem: A home health nurse visits a 76-year-old client with right hemiplegia and decreased sensation on the right side after a stroke. The client's adult daughter provides care. Which statements by the daughter indicate a need for further teaching? Select all that apply.
options: “I rub lotion firmly into the red areas over her tailbone.”
“I put a pillow lengthwise under her calves so her heels float.”
“She sits on a rubber ring cushion when she is in the recliner.”
“She stays on her right side most of the day since she can't feel that side.”
“I offer her a protein shake between her meals.”
“I sprinkle cornstarch in her groin after she is incontinent.”
optionRationales: Correct — needs teaching. Massage over reddened bony prominences damages fragile capillaries and worsens deep injury.
Incorrect — correct practice. Floating the heels offloads a high-risk prominence.
Correct — needs teaching. Ring (doughnut) cushions press on the surrounding tissue and reduce blood flow.
Correct — needs teaching. Lost sensation is a risk factor, not protection: she cannot feel the warning discomfort, so she needs scheduled repositioning at least every 2 hours.
Incorrect — correct practice. Extra protein and calories support skin integrity.
Correct — needs teaching. Cornstarch clumps when wet and irritates skin; the slides list it as a product to avoid.
questions.rationale: This teaching evaluation relies on the risk-factor lesson. Diminished sensation after a stroke means the client cannot feel the discomfort that would normally prompt a position change. Leaving her on the numb side is therefore dangerous, not safe. Massage, ring cushions, and cornstarch are on the slides' avoid list. Floating the heels and giving protein supplements are correct prevention.
questions.takeaway: Numb side = can't feel the warning; reposition on a schedule and avoid massage, rings, and powders.
questions.hintContent: Recall why diminished sensation raises risk and the prevention practices the slides say to avoid.
questions.hintStrategy: This item is negatively worded: you are selecting the statements that are WRONG. Judge each statement on its own as safe or unsafe.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Exemplar 21.B Pressure Injuries · RYB Wound Care & Debridement
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.stem: The nurse is comparing this week's assessment of a client's Stage 3 sacral pressure injury with last week's documentation. Which findings indicate the wound is progressing toward healing? Select all that apply.
options: Undermining now extends 2 cm (previously 1 cm)
Wound length decreased from 5.0 cm to 3.8 cm
Moderate thick, green drainage with a foul odor after cleansing
Beefy red, granular tissue covers 90% of the wound bed
Periwound skin is white and wrinkled
New pink epithelial tissue along the wound margin
optionRationales: Incorrect. Increasing undermining means more tissue destruction beneath the edges.
Correct. Decreasing dimensions measured the same way each week show the wound is filling and contracting.
Incorrect. Thick, green, foul-smelling drainage is purulent and suggests infection.
Correct. Healthy granulation tissue is beefy red, moist, and granular.
Incorrect. White, wrinkled periwound skin is maceration from excess moisture.
Correct. Epithelial cells migrating from the margin are the final step in wound closure.
questions.rationale: Evaluating a wound combines three lessons. Beefy red granulation is healthy proliferative-phase tissue (the RYB goal is to protect it). Shrinking length and a pink epithelial rim at the margins show the wound is closing by secondary intention. Growing undermining means more tissue destruction. Thick, green, foul-smelling (purulent) drainage suggests infection. White, wrinkled periwound skin is maceration from excess moisture.
questions.takeaway: Healing = smaller, redder, pink edges; worsening = deeper undermining, purulent drainage, macerated edges.
questions.hintContent: Recall what healthy granulation and epithelialization look like in the proliferative phase and what purulent exudate and maceration mean.
questions.hintStrategy: Compare each finding with last week or with normal healing. Select only the findings that show change in the right direction.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Exemplar 21.B Pressure Injuries · Pathophysiology & Risk Factors
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.stem: A client on bed rest with pneumonia has a temperature of 39.2 °C (102.6 °F). A nursing student asks how the fever affects the client's pressure-injury risk and care. Which response by the nurse is accurate?
options: “Fever lowers capillary pressure to zero, so turning can wait until the fever breaks.”
“Fever thickens the skin and makes it less elastic, so massage the bony prominences.”
“Fever causes the kidneys to lose protein, so protein should be limited until it resolves.”
“Fever raises oxygen demand, so compressed tissue turns ischemic sooner; keep turning.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. Fever does not drop capillary pressure to zero, and delaying turns lengthens ischemia.
Incorrect. Fever does not thicken skin, and massage over bony prominences damages tissue.
Incorrect. Fever does not cause protein loss through the kidneys, and restricting protein would weaken tissue and slow healing.
Correct. Heat raises the metabolic rate and oxygen demand, so tissue under pressure runs out of oxygen sooner. Repositioning at least every 2 hours is even more important.
questions.rationale: Excessive body heat is a slide risk factor because it raises the metabolic rate and oxygen demand. Tissue already squeezed over a bony prominence becomes ischemic faster. The prevention response is to keep up scheduled repositioning, not delay it. Massage and protein restriction contradict the prevention lesson.
questions.takeaway: Fever speeds ischemia under pressure, so never let the turning schedule slip in a febrile client.
questions.hintContent: Recall how temperature affects cellular metabolism and oxygen demand, and the repositioning schedule for bed-bound clients.
questions.hintStrategy: Each option has two parts, a mechanism and an action. Both parts must be correct.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Exemplar 21.B Pressure Injuries · Pathophysiology & Risk Factors
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care
questions.stem: The nurse on a medical-surgical unit is reviewing four assigned clients. Which client should the nurse prioritize for pressure-injury prevention measures?
options: A 45-year-old with a casted wrist fracture who walks independently and eats 100% of every meal
A 29-year-old with a new T4 spinal cord injury, fever of 38.9 °C (102 °F), and bowel incontinence
A 70-year-old with heart failure who walks in the hall three times daily and is continent of urine
A 62-year-old with diabetes who sits in a chair most of the day and shifts position independently
optionRationales: Incorrect. Independent ambulation and adequate intake mean low risk despite the fracture.
Correct. Absent sensation and mobility below T4, excess body heat raising oxygen demand, and moisture from incontinence combine several major risk factors.
Incorrect. Age and heart failure raise risk slightly, but this client is mobile and continent.
Incorrect. Sitting increases ischial pressure, but the client can sense discomfort and shift weight independently.
questions.rationale: When choosing which client is at greatest risk, look for stacked risk factors. The client with a new T4 spinal cord injury has lost both sensation and movement below the injury, so he cannot feel or relieve pressure. Fever raises oxygen demand, and bowel incontinence adds moisture and enzymes. The other clients can walk or shift their own weight.
questions.takeaway: Greatest risk = the most risk factors stacked together, especially lost sensation plus immobility.
questions.hintContent: Recall the slide risk factors and which ones affect both the ability to feel pressure and the ability to move away from it.
questions.hintStrategy: Count the risk factors for each client. Then ask which client cannot feel the pressure or move away from it.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Exemplar 21.B Pressure Injuries · Pathophysiology & Risk Factors
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.stem: A 72-year-old client was found on the floor at home after lying on the right side for about 10 hours. The skin over the right hip is intact and red, and it does not blanch when pressed. Which explanation by the nurse to the family is accurate?
options: “Pressure above capillary pressure cut off blood flow; this Stage 1 injury can still heal.”
“Pressure made fluid build up and thickened the skin; this is normal redness that will fade soon.”
“The redness means the tissue is already recovering; this is a Stage 2 injury because the skin is red.”
“Lying still let collagen collect in the hip; this is a Stage 3 injury because the redness is deep.”
optionRationales: Correct. External pressure above about 32 mm Hg closed the capillaries, and the tissue became ischemic. Intact, nonblanchable redness is Stage 1, which can resolve if pressure is relieved.
Incorrect. Pressure does not strengthen skin, and redness that does not blanch is not normal reactive redness.
Incorrect. Nonblanchable redness signals damage, not recovery. Stage 2 requires partial-thickness skin loss or a blister.
Incorrect. Collagen does not collect from immobility, and Stage 3 requires full-thickness loss into fat.
questions.rationale: The explanation combines pathophysiology and staging. Prolonged pressure greater than capillary pressure (about 32 mm Hg) reduces blood flow, causing ischemia; unrelieved, this leads to necrosis and ulceration. On intact skin, redness that does not blanch is a Stage 1 injury. It is the last point at which the injury can be reversed by keeping pressure off the area.
questions.takeaway: Pressure > 32 mm Hg → ischemia; nonblanchable redness on intact skin = Stage 1, still reversible.
questions.hintContent: Recall the capillary pressure value, the pressure → ischemia → necrosis → ulcer pathway, and what defines Stage 1.
questions.hintStrategy: Check both halves of each option: the mechanism and the stage. Eliminate an option if either half is wrong.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Exemplar 21.B Pressure Injuries · Pathophysiology & Risk Factors
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing data for an 88-year-old resident of a long-term care facility who has advanced dementia. Which findings increase this resident's risk for pressure injury? Select all that apply.
options: Weight decreased from 54 kg (119 lb) to 49 kg (108 lb) over the past month
Needs moderate assistance to move in bed and slides down in the wheelchair
Incontinent of urine several times per shift
Walks to the dining room with a walker three times daily
Hemoglobin 13.8 g/dL
Drinks about 1,800 mL of fluid daily
optionRationales: Correct. A 9% loss in 1 month signals malnutrition, loss of padding over bony prominences, and poor tissue repair.
Correct. Limited mobility and sliding produce sustained pressure plus friction and shear.
Correct. Urine moisture macerates skin and lowers its tolerance to pressure and friction.
Incorrect. Regular ambulation is protective.
Incorrect. This hemoglobin is within normal limits and supports oxygen delivery.
Incorrect. Adequate fluid intake supports skin turgor and perfusion.
questions.rationale: The slides tie risk to the Braden areas and to nutrition markers. Losing 5 kg (about 9%) in a month signals inadequate nutrition, meaning less padding and weaker tissue. Needing help to move and sliding in the wheelchair reflect limited mobility plus shear. Frequent incontinence adds moisture that macerates skin. Walking three times daily, a normal hemoglobin, and adequate fluid intake are protective.
questions.takeaway: Weight loss, limited mobility with sliding, and incontinence are classic stacked risks in long-term care.
questions.hintContent: Recall the Braden subscales and the nutrition values (weight, hemoglobin, albumin, lymphocytes) the slides say to monitor.
questions.hintStrategy: Decide whether each value is normal or abnormal, then whether it maps to a risk factor. Normal values and activity are not risks.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Exemplar 21.B Pressure Injuries · Pathophysiology & Risk Factors
questions.clientNeed: Health Promotion and Maintenance
questions.stem: The daughter of an 86-year-old client asks why her mother developed a pressure injury after only 2 days in bed with a hip fracture. Which explanation by the nurse is most accurate?
options: “Aging skin is thinner and less elastic, with less oil, padding, and blood flow.”
“Older adults sweat much more than younger adults, so the skin under her stays soaked with moisture.”
“Aging thickens the outer layer of skin, and that thicker layer traps heat against the tissue underneath.”
“Older adults have higher capillary pressure, so the mattress presses harder on the skin over the bones.”
optionRationales: Correct. Older skin is thinner, drier, less elastic, and less cushioned, with poorer circulation, so it breaks down faster under pressure and heals more slowly.
Incorrect. Sweating decreases with age; older skin is typically drier.
Incorrect. The epidermis thins with age, and heat is not trapped by a thickened layer.
Incorrect. Higher capillary pressure would protect the tissue, not endanger it; age does not raise capillary pressure.
questions.rationale: Advanced age is a slide risk factor because of changes in skin structure. The epidermis and dermis thin, oil and moisture decrease, subcutaneous padding shrinks, and circulation declines. Tissue therefore becomes ischemic and breaks down under pressure faster, and it heals more slowly. Immobility from the hip fracture adds to these changes.
questions.takeaway: Older skin = thin, dry, less padded, less perfused, so it breaks down sooner.
questions.hintContent: Recall how the epidermis, dermis, oil glands, and subcutaneous fat change with aging.
questions.hintStrategy: Eliminate options that describe the opposite of known age-related skin changes.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Exemplar 21.B Pressure Injuries · Prevention
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort
questions.stem: A client on bed rest has a Stage 2 pressure injury on the sacrum and an area of nonblanchable erythema over the right greater trochanter. The nurse is about to turn the client off the back. Which position is most appropriate?
options: Left side-lying at 90° with the top leg resting directly on the bottom leg
Supine with the head of the bed at 45° and the knees gatched for comfort
Left 30° lateral tilt with pillows behind the back and between the knees
Right 30° lateral tilt so the client can face the door and reach the call light
optionRationales: Incorrect. A 90° side-lying position places full body weight on the left trochanter, and the legs touching creates pressure between bony knees and ankles.
Incorrect. This keeps the client on the injured sacrum and increases shear with HOB above 30°.
Correct. A 30° tilt to the left relieves the sacrum and the injured right trochanter without loading the left trochanter directly; pillows keep bony prominences apart.
Incorrect. Tilting to the right loads the right trochanter, which already has a Stage 1 injury.
questions.rationale: Positioning depends on staging. The client has a Stage 2 injury on the sacrum and a Stage 1 injury (nonblanchable redness) over the right trochanter, and the slides say not to position a client on an existing injury. A left 30° lateral tilt with pillows behind the back puts weight on the fleshy left buttock and spares both injured sites. Pillows between the knees keep bone off bone. A 90° side-lying position loads the trochanter, and a HOB at 45° increases sacral shear.
questions.takeaway: Never position on an injury; a 30° tilt toward the uninjured side spares the sacrum and hip.
questions.hintContent: Recall which bony prominence bears weight in each position and the stage of each of this client's injuries.
questions.hintStrategy: Identify both injured sites first, then eliminate any position that loads either one.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Exemplar 21.B Pressure Injuries · Prevention
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort
questions.stem: An 80-year-old client with heart failure and limited mobility at a rehabilitation facility prefers to sit up in a chair for much of the day. The client can follow simple directions. Which interventions should the nurse include to protect the client's skin while sitting? Select all that apply.
options: Reposition the client at least every hour while in the chair
Use a seating cushion designed to redistribute pressure
Place a foam ring cushion under the buttocks
Support the feet on the floor or a footrest so the thighs are level
Recline the chair so the client slides forward off the sacrum
Cue the client to shift weight about every 15 minutes
optionRationales: Correct. Seated clients bear high ischial pressure and should be repositioned at least every hour.
Correct. Pressure-redistributing cushions reduce peak pressure on the ischial tuberosities.
Incorrect. Ring cushions reduce blood flow to the surrounding tissue and are avoided.
Correct. Supported feet and level thighs spread weight across the thighs instead of the ischia and prevent sliding.
Incorrect. Sliding forward creates shear across the sacrum and coccyx.
Correct. Clients who are able should shift weight every 15–30 minutes (commonly taught as every 15 minutes).
questions.rationale: Sitting concentrates body weight on the small ischial tuberosities, and a reclined or slumped posture adds shear. The slides therefore call for repositioning every hour in a chair and weight shifts about every 15 minutes, using a pressure-redistributing cushion (never a ring) and keeping the feet supported so the thighs are level. Ring cushions reduce blood flow to the surrounding tissue, and sliding forward creates shear.
questions.takeaway: Chair: reposition hourly, shift weight every 15 minutes, use a real cushion, keep feet supported, no rings.
questions.hintContent: Recall the chair repositioning times and how sliding in a chair produces shear.
questions.hintStrategy: For each option, ask whether it reduces pressure on the sitting bones without adding shear or narrowing blood flow.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Exemplar 21.B Pressure Injuries · Prevention
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care
questions.stem: The RN is observing an LPN provide care to a client at high risk for pressure injury. Which action by the LPN requires the RN's immediate intervention?
options: Raising the head of the bed to 30° after the client finishes lunch
Using a draw sheet with a UAP to move the client up in bed
Massaging lotion into a reddened area over the client's sacrum
Applying a dimethicone barrier cream after perineal care
optionRationales: Appropriate. Keeping the HOB at 30° or lower reduces shear.
Appropriate. Lifting with a draw sheet avoids friction and shear.
Requires intervention. Massage over bony prominences or reddened areas damages capillaries and deeper tissue and is avoided.
Appropriate. Barrier creams such as dimethicone protect skin from moisture.
questions.rationale: The RN supervises care delegated to the LPN. Massage over a reddened bony prominence can break fragile capillaries and worsen deep damage, so the RN must stop it immediately. The other actions follow prevention guidelines: HOB at 30° after meals, lifting with a draw sheet, and applying a barrier cream.
questions.takeaway: Stop anyone massaging a reddened bony prominence.
questions.hintContent: Recall which skin-care practices the slides list under 'avoid' and the RN's supervisory role.
questions.hintStrategy: Three options are safe prevention measures. Find the one that could cause harm.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Exemplar 21.B Pressure Injuries · Prevention
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort
questions.stem: A 74-year-old client has a Stage 3 sacral pressure injury, eats about 50% of meals, and has lost 4 kg (8.8 lb) in a month. Serum albumin is 2.9 g/dL, and kidney function is normal. Which intervention is the priority to support wound healing?
options: Restrict fluids to 1,000 mL/day to reduce drainage from the wound
Offer high-calorie, high-protein supplements between meals
Limit protein to prevent weight gain while the client is on bed rest
Provide a low-calorie diet so the client can reposition more easily
optionRationales: Incorrect. Limiting fluids does not usefully dry a wound; adequate hydration keeps tissue perfused and supple.
Correct. Weight loss, poor intake, and albumin below 3.5 g/dL show malnutrition. Healing needs more protein and calories, and supplements fill the gap between meals.
Incorrect. Protein is the building block for collagen and new tissue; restricting it slows healing.
Incorrect. Too few calories makes the body burn protein for energy instead of using it to build tissue.
questions.rationale: The low albumin, weight loss, and poor intake together show malnutrition, which delays healing. The prevention and health-promotion slides call for more protein, calories, vitamins A and C, zinc, and iron, with supplements when intake is poor, plus a dietitian consult. Fluid, protein, and calorie restrictions work against healing in a client with normal kidney function.
questions.takeaway: Low albumin + weight loss in a client with a wound → more protein and calories, never less.
questions.hintContent: Recall the albumin threshold for delayed healing and the nutrients a healing wound needs.
questions.hintStrategy: Interpret the lab and weight data first. Then pick the option that gives the tissue more of what it lacks.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Exemplar 21.B Pressure Injuries · Prevention
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care
questions.stem: The RN is supervising a UAP who is providing morning care to a client with a Braden score of 12 on a low-air-loss mattress. Which actions by the UAP require the RN to intervene? Select all that apply.
options: Bathing the client with hot water to stimulate circulation
Placing three folded incontinence pads under the client on the mattress
Using a lift sheet with a coworker to reposition the client
Applying a dimethicone barrier cream after perineal care
Dusting cornstarch into the skin folds under the abdomen
Reporting a red area that has not faded 30 minutes after turning
optionRationales: Intervene. Hot water dries and damages the skin; use warm water and mild cleansers.
Intervene. Multiple linen layers block the airflow and pressure redistribution of a low-air-loss surface.
Appropriate. A lift sheet with two people prevents friction and shear.
Appropriate. Dimethicone barrier products protect skin from moisture.
Intervene. Powders and cornstarch clump with moisture and irritate the skin.
Appropriate. Persistent redness should be reported so the RN can assess it.
questions.rationale: The RN keeps accountability for care delegated to the UAP and must correct unsafe practice. Hot water dries and damages fragile skin. Stacked pads create ridges and block the air flow of a low-air-loss surface. Cornstarch clumps and irritates skin in folds. Lifting with a sheet, applying dimethicone, and reporting redness that does not fade are correct actions.
questions.takeaway: No hot water, no stacked pads, no powder — and praise UAPs who report redness that doesn't fade.
questions.hintContent: Recall the skin-hygiene avoid list and how a low-air-loss surface should be used.
questions.hintStrategy: You are selecting UNSAFE actions. Judge each action separately as safe or unsafe.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Exemplar 21.B Pressure Injuries · Prevention
questions.clientNeed: Health Promotion and Maintenance
questions.stem: A 34-year-old client with a T8 spinal cord injury who uses a manual wheelchair is being discharged home. Which client statement indicates a need for further teaching about pressure-injury prevention?
options: “I'll use a long-handled mirror every day to check my buttocks and heels.”
“I'll do a lean or push-up to shift my weight about every 15 minutes in my chair.”
“Since I can't feel my buttocks, I'll shift my weight when I start to feel uncomfortable.”
“If a red spot doesn't fade 30 minutes after I'm off it, I'll stay off it and call the clinic.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. Daily self-inspection with a mirror detects early injury in areas the client cannot see or feel.
Incorrect. Frequent weight shifts relieve ischial pressure.
Correct. The client lacks sensation below T8 and cannot rely on discomfort; weight shifts must be done on a schedule.
Incorrect. Persistent redness means injury; the area must be offloaded and evaluated.
questions.rationale: Diminished sensation is a risk factor because the client cannot feel the discomfort that normally prompts movement. A client with a T8 injury therefore has to shift weight on a schedule (about every 15 minutes in the chair), not when discomfort occurs. Daily mirror checks and staying off a red area that does not fade show correct understanding.
questions.takeaway: No sensation = no warning; weight shifts go by the clock, not by feel.
questions.hintContent: Recall why diminished sensation raises risk and the weight-shift interval for wheelchair users.
questions.hintStrategy: Look for a statement that depends on a sense the client no longer has.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Exemplar 21.B Pressure Injuries · Prevention
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.stem: A client on bed rest has been lying supine for most of the shift. Which bony prominences should the nurse inspect most closely for pressure injury? Select all that apply.
options: Occiput
Sacrum and coccyx
Heels
Anterior knees
Forehead and chin
Scapulae
optionRationales: Correct. The back of the head bears weight in the supine position.
Correct. The sacrum and coccyx are the most common pressure sites when supine.
Correct. The heels rest directly on the mattress when supine unless they are floated.
Incorrect. The anterior knees bear weight in the prone position.
Incorrect. The forehead and chin bear weight in the prone position.
Correct. The shoulder blades bear weight in the supine position.
questions.rationale: The prominences at risk depend on position. When supine, weight rests on the occiput, scapulae, elbows, sacrum and coccyx, and heels, so these areas are inspected closely under good light. The anterior knees, forehead, and chin bear weight in the prone position, not supine.
questions.takeaway: Supine: back of head, shoulder blades, elbows, sacrum and coccyx, heels.
questions.hintContent: Recall which bony prominences bear weight in each position.
questions.hintStrategy: Picture the client lying on the back and select only the prominences touching the mattress.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Exemplar 21.B Pressure Injuries · Prevention
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort
questions.stem: A client at high risk for pressure injury is incontinent of liquid stool. The nurse has performed hand hygiene, applied clean gloves, and removed the soiled pad. Which action should the nurse take next?
options: Cleanse the perineal skin gently with a mild cleanser and warm water
Apply a thin layer of barrier cream such as dimethicone
Pat the skin dry without rubbing
Place a single breathable underpad and reposition the client off the sacrum
optionRationales: Correct. The irritant is removed first with gentle cleansing using a mild agent and warm (not hot) water.
Incorrect. A barrier is applied only after the skin is cleansed and dried.
Incorrect. The skin is patted dry after it is cleansed.
Incorrect. A fresh pad is placed and the client repositioned after the skin is cleansed, dried, and protected.
questions.rationale: Remove the irritant promptly, cleanse gently with a mild agent and warm (not hot) water, pat dry to avoid friction, and protect the skin with a barrier before placing a single breathable pad and repositioning. This protects skin from moisture and enzymes that cause maceration.
questions.takeaway: Remove → cleanse → pat dry → protect → reposition.
questions.hintContent: Recall the sequence of incontinence care that protects the skin from moisture and enzymes.
questions.hintStrategy: All four actions belong in the procedure. Pick the one that must be done before the others make sense.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Exemplar 21.B Pressure Injuries · Four Stages of Pressure Injuries
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.stem: After cleansing, the nurse assesses a client's coccyx wound, which measures 3 × 2 × 0.5 cm. The bed has red granulation tissue and visible yellow fat, and soft, stringy yellow tissue covers about 20% of the base. No muscle, tendon, or bone is visible or palpable. Which documentation and plan are correct?
options: Stage 4; debride the base because yellow tissue is present in the wound
Stage 3; cleanse to remove the soft, stringy yellow nonviable tissue
Stage 2; protect the red granulation and leave the yellow tissue in place
Stage 3; protect both the yellow fat and the yellow tissue from trauma
optionRationales: Incorrect. Stage 4 requires visible or palpable muscle, tendon, or bone. Slough affects treatment, not stage.
Correct. Visible fat without deeper structures is Stage 3. Soft, stringy yellow tissue is slough, and the RYB goal for yellow is to cleanse it away.
Incorrect. Visible fat means full-thickness loss, which is beyond Stage 2, and slough should be removed.
Incorrect. The stage is correct, but slough is dead tissue that must be cleansed away; only living tissue (red granulation and fat) is protected.
questions.rationale: The deepest visible tissue sets the stage: fat without muscle, tendon, or bone is Stage 3. The color of the tissue sets the treatment goal. Soft, stringy yellow tissue is slough (dead tissue), so the RYB goal is to cleanse it; red granulation is protected. Students must tell yellow fat (living tissue, a staging clue) from yellow slough (dead tissue, a treatment clue).
questions.takeaway: Deepest tissue = stage; tissue color = treatment. Yellow fat is living; yellow slough is dead.
questions.hintContent: Recall the tissue that defines Stage 3 versus Stage 4 and the RYB goal for each color.
questions.hintStrategy: Answer two questions separately, what stage and what goal, then find the option that gets both right.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Exemplar 21.B Pressure Injuries · Four Stages of Pressure Injuries
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.stem: A 75-year-old client on bed rest has a Braden score of 12. The skin is intact, and all reddened areas blanch and fade after turning. Which nursing diagnosis best describes the client's skin?
options: Potential for impaired skin integrity
Risk for infection related to an open wound
Impaired skin integrity
Situational low self-esteem
optionRationales: Correct. A high-risk Braden score with intact skin fits a potential (risk) diagnosis.
Incorrect. There is no open wound.
Incorrect. The skin is intact; there is no actual impairment yet.
Incorrect. Nothing in the data suggests a problem with self-esteem.
questions.rationale: Three steps lead to the answer. A Braden score of 12 means high risk. Redness that blanches and fades is normal reactive redness, not a Stage 1 injury, so no pressure injury is present. With high risk and intact skin, the correct nursing diagnosis is potential for impaired skin integrity. Impaired skin integrity and risk for infection require an actual break or injury.
questions.takeaway: High risk + intact, blanchable skin = potential for impaired skin integrity.
questions.hintContent: Recall what blanchable redness means for staging and how the slide diagnoses differ for intact versus injured skin.
questions.hintStrategy: First decide whether an injury exists. Then choose the diagnosis that matches actual versus potential.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Exemplar 21.B Pressure Injuries · Four Stages of Pressure Injuries
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing skin findings recorded for several clients. Which findings should be classified as a Stage 2 pressure injury? Select all that apply.
options: Intact skin over the sacrum with redness that does not blanch
Shallow open wound with a pink, moist bed over the ischial tuberosity of a client who sits all day
Full-thickness wound over the hip with visible yellow fat
Intact blister filled with clear fluid on the heel of a client on bed rest
Ruptured blister over the elbow with a moist, pink base
optionRationales: Incorrect. Intact skin with nonblanchable redness is Stage 1.
Correct. Partial-thickness loss with a shallow, pink, moist bed is Stage 2.
Incorrect. Visible fat means full-thickness loss — Stage 3.
Correct. A clear-fluid blister is partial-thickness loss of the epidermis.
Correct. A ruptured blister with a pink, moist base is partial-thickness loss.
questions.rationale: Stage 2 is partial-thickness loss of the epidermis and possibly the dermis. It appears as a clear-fluid blister (intact or ruptured) or as a shallow, pink, moist open area. Knowing the skin layers explains the distinction. Intact skin with nonblanchable redness is still Stage 1, and visible subcutaneous fat means full-thickness loss (Stage 3).
questions.takeaway: Blister (intact or broken) or shallow pink moist wound = Stage 2.
questions.hintContent: Recall the layers of the skin and which layers are lost in each stage.
questions.hintStrategy: For each finding, ask which layer is the deepest one involved, then match it to the stage.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Exemplar 21.B Pressure Injuries · Prevention
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing pressure-redistribution devices with a newly hired UAP who will care for a client at high risk for pressure injury. Which instruction should the nurse give the UAP?
options: “Place a doughnut (ring) cushion under the sacrum when the client sits up.”
“Wrap the client's ankles snugly with elastic bandages to protect the heels.”
“Place a rolled towel directly under each heel so it is cushioned against the surface of the bed.”
“Use heel protectors or pillows under the calves so the heels are lifted off the bed.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. Doughnut devices reduce blood flow to the surrounding tissue and cause injury.
Incorrect. Tight wraps around the ankles impair circulation and do not offload the heels.
Incorrect. A towel under the heel still concentrates pressure on the heel.
Correct. Heel protectors or pillows that float the heels offload these high-risk pressure points.
questions.rationale: The goal of supportive devices is to keep external pressure below capillary pressure (32 mm Hg). Overlays, specialty beds, pillows, wedges, and heel protectors offload pressure points and reduce pressure injuries by about 60%. Doughnut devices reduce blood flow and cause injury, so they are avoided.
questions.takeaway: Keep pressure < 32 mm Hg; float heels; no doughnuts.
questions.hintContent: Recall which supportive devices offload pressure points and which device the slides say to avoid.
questions.hintStrategy: Ask whether each device removes pressure from the skin or concentrates or restricts it.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Exemplar 21.B Pressure Injuries · Four Stages of Pressure Injuries
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.stem: The nurse is measuring and assessing a client's sacral pressure injury after cleansing. Which findings, if present, would indicate that the wound is a Stage 4 pressure injury? Select all that apply.
options: Bone palpable at the base with a sterile applicator
Visible tendon in the wound bed
Visible subcutaneous fat with no deeper structures
Exposed muscle at the base
Undermining of 1 cm beneath the lower wound edge
Red, moist granulation tissue along the wound walls
optionRationales: Correct. Palpable or exposed bone is Stage 4.
Correct. Exposed tendon, a supporting structure, is Stage 4.
Incorrect. Visible fat without deeper structures is Stage 3.
Correct. Exposed muscle is Stage 4.
Incorrect. Undermining can occur in deep wounds of either Stage 3 or Stage 4; it does not define the stage.
Incorrect. Granulation tissue shows healing activity, not the depth of the original injury.
questions.rationale: Stage 4 means full-thickness loss with muscle, tendon (a supporting structure), or bone seen or felt, often with a sterile applicator during the depth measurement. Undermining and granulation are wound features that the nurse documents during assessment, but they do not set the stage. Visible fat alone is Stage 3.
questions.takeaway: Stage 4 = muscle, tendon, or bone; undermining and granulation don't change the stage.
questions.hintContent: Recall the deepest tissue for each stage and which documented features describe a wound without staging it.
questions.hintStrategy: Select only the findings that name a structure deeper than fat.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Exemplar 21.B Pressure Injuries · Nursing Process
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care
questions.stem: The nurse receives hand-off report for four clients on a medical unit. Which client should the nurse assess first?
options: A client with a Stage 2 sacral pressure injury whose dressing edge is rolled
A client with a Braden score of 12 who was last repositioned 2½ hours ago and reports sacral soreness
A client with a Stage 3 sacral pressure injury who is scheduled for a dressing change this morning
A client with a Stage 4 sacral pressure injury who is newly confused, with HR 116 and BP 88/50
optionRationales: Not first. A rolled edge needs attention soon but is not life-threatening.
Not first. This client needs repositioning promptly (which can be delegated), but the condition is not an immediate threat to life.
Not first. A routine scheduled dressing change is stable care.
First. New confusion, tachycardia, and hypotension in a client with a deep wound suggest a spreading, systemic infection — a life-threatening complication.
questions.rationale: Unstable before stable. New confusion, tachycardia, and hypotension in a client with a deep pressure injury suggest the wound infection is spreading through the body, and this is a threat to perfusion. The complications lesson teaches that infection shows up as systemic signs, so this client is assessed first and the provider notified. The overdue turn can be delegated to the UAP, and the rolled dressing edge and routine dressing change can wait.
questions.takeaway: Deep wound + new confusion + low BP + tachycardia = possible spreading infection → assess first.
questions.hintContent: Recall the systemic signs of a spreading wound infection and the unstable-before-stable principle.
questions.hintStrategy: Look for abnormal vital signs and a change in mental status. That is the client who cannot wait.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Exemplar 21.B Pressure Injuries · Nursing Process
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care
questions.stem: The RN is making assignments with an LPN on a medical-surgical unit. Which task related to pressure-injury care is most appropriate to assign to the LPN?
options: Performing the prescribed dressing change on a Stage 3 wound staged by the RN today
Completing the initial admission skin assessment and staging for a newly admitted client
Developing the pressure-injury prevention teaching plan for a client going home today
Determining the stage of a new open area found on a client's heel
optionRationales: Correct. Performing an established, prescribed dressing change on a stable client is within LPN scope; the LPN reports changes to the RN.
Incorrect. The initial admission assessment and staging are RN responsibilities.
Incorrect. Developing a teaching plan requires RN-level planning; the LPN may reinforce teaching.
Incorrect. Interpreting and staging a new finding is an RN assessment.
questions.rationale: Staging requires RN assessment and judgment. An LPN can perform an established, prescribed dressing change on a stable client whose wound the RN has already assessed and staged. Admission assessment, staging a new wound, and creating a teaching plan remain with the RN.
questions.takeaway: RN stages and plans; LPN performs established dressing changes on already-staged, stable wounds.
questions.hintContent: Recall which parts of pressure-injury care require RN judgment (assess, stage, plan, evaluate).
questions.hintStrategy: Eliminate any task that involves first-time assessment, staging, or planning.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Exemplar 21.B Pressure Injuries · Nursing Process
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care
questions.stem: The nurse is writing expected outcomes for a client with a Stage 3 sacral pressure injury. Which outcome statements are correctly written? Select all that apply.
options: The client will state three ways to protect the skin before discharge.
The sacral wound will decrease in length and width by 25% within 2 weeks.
The nurse will turn the client every 2 hours.
The client will understand the importance of good nutrition.
The client will have no new areas of nonblanchable erythema during hospitalization.
The client’s wound will heal quickly.
optionRationales: Correct. Client-centered, measurable (three ways), and time-bound (before discharge).
Correct. Measurable (25%) and time-bound (2 weeks).
Incorrect. This is a nursing intervention written about the nurse, not a client outcome.
Incorrect. ‘Understand’ is not observable or measurable.
Correct. Measurable and time-bound; it reflects prevention of further breakdown.
Incorrect. ‘Quickly’ is vague and has no measurable criterion or time frame.
questions.rationale: Expected outcomes are client-centered, specific, measurable, realistic, and time-limited. Interventions describe what the nurse does, and verbs like ‘understand’ or vague words like ‘quickly’ cannot be evaluated.
questions.takeaway: Outcomes: the client will [measurable verb] [criterion] by [time].
questions.hintContent: Recall the parts of a well-written outcome: subject, measurable verb, criterion, and time frame.
questions.hintStrategy: For each statement, ask ‘Who is the subject?’ and ‘How would I measure this?’

questions.ref: Module 21 · Exemplar 21.B Pressure Injuries · Nursing Process
questions.clientNeed: Psychosocial Integrity
questions.stem: A 67-year-old client with a Stage 4 sacral pressure injury tells the nurse, “I can smell my own wound. I don't want my grandchildren to visit anymore.” Which response by the nurse is most appropriate?
options: “The odor comes from bacteria, so it's safer if the children don't visit for now.”
“Try not to worry. Most visitors don't notice the smell at all.”
“You sound embarrassed. Let's plan ways to control the odor before they visit.”
“I'll spray some air freshener around the room before your visitors arrive.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. This reinforces isolation and is not accurate; standard precautions and a covered wound protect visitors.
Incorrect. False reassurance dismisses the client’s feelings and closes communication.
Correct. Reflecting the feeling acknowledges compromised dignity, and planning odor control (timely cleansing and dressing changes) addresses the cause.
Incorrect. Masking odor does not address the client’s feelings or the source of odor, and sprays can irritate.
questions.rationale: Pressure injuries can cause compromised dignity and situational low self-esteem. Therapeutic communication acknowledges the feeling and involves the client in solutions such as timely wound cleansing and dressing changes.
questions.takeaway: Acknowledge the feeling, then solve the problem together.
questions.hintContent: Recall the psychosocial nursing diagnoses associated with pressure injuries and the features of therapeutic responses.
questions.hintStrategy: Eliminate responses that give false reassurance, change the subject, or promote isolation.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Exemplar 21.B Pressure Injuries · Nursing Process
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation

tabs.title: Care Plan
tabs.html:
• Reposition every 2 hours; low-air-loss mattress
  • Cleanse with normal saline and apply a moist dressing daily
  • Oral nutrition supplement twice daily

questions.stem: Refer to the Wound Measurements and Care Plan for a client with a Stage 3 sacral pressure injury. Based on the nurse's evaluation, which action is the priority?
options: Continue the current plan unchanged for another month
Reassess the client and wound and collaborate with the team to revise the plan
Switch to a doughnut cushion to fully offload the sacrum
Document that the wound is healing by primary intention and continue weekly monitoring as expected
optionRationales: Incorrect. The wound has deteriorated over 2 weeks; continuing an ineffective plan delays healing.
Correct. When goals are not met, the nurse reassesses and modifies the care plan; no progress over about 2 weeks calls for this.
Incorrect. Doughnut cushions reduce blood flow to surrounding tissue and are harmful.
Incorrect. Pressure injuries heal by secondary intention, and this wound is getting worse, not healing.
questions.rationale: Over 2 weeks the wound has grown larger and deeper, the yellow slough has increased from 20% to 40% (less healthy red tissue by RYB standards), and drainage has increased. A pressure injury heals by secondary intention and should be getting smaller and redder. When goals are not met, the nurse reassesses the client and wound, including positioning, the support surface, and nutrition, and works with the team to revise the plan.
questions.takeaway: Bigger, deeper, more slough over 2 weeks = the plan is failing; reassess and revise.
questions.hintContent: Recall what a healing secondary-intention wound should look like over time and what increasing slough means in the RYB system.
questions.hintStrategy: Compare week 1 with week 3 for size, color, and drainage. Decide the trend, then pick the action that fits it.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Exemplar 21.B Pressure Injuries · Prevention
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.stem: The nurse reviews new prescriptions for a client with a Stage 2 sacral pressure injury. Which prescription is the priority for the nurse to clarify with the provider before implementing it?
options: Reposition at least every 2 hours using pillows and wedges for support
Dietitian consult for protein and calorie supplements
Apply heel protectors while the client is in bed
Place a doughnut cushion under the sacrum when the client sits up
optionRationales: Appropriate. Repositioning at least every 2 hours with positioning devices is a standard outcome and intervention.
Appropriate. Supplements and dietitian input support healing when intake is poor.
Appropriate. Heel protectors offload the heels.
Clarify. Doughnut devices reduce blood flow to the surrounding tissue and cause injury; a pressure-redistributing seat cushion is used instead.
questions.rationale: The doughnut cushion is the prescription to clarify. Ring devices press on the tissue surrounding the hole, cutting off blood flow to the area they are meant to protect, and in a client who already has a Stage 2 injury they cause ischemic damage. Repositioning with pillows and wedges, a dietitian consult, and heel protectors are appropriate prevention.
questions.takeaway: Doughnut devices always get questioned: they reduce blood flow and cause injury.
questions.hintContent: Recall how external pressure affects capillary blood flow and which devices the slides say to avoid.
questions.hintStrategy: Three prescriptions are standard prevention. Find the one that could cause harm.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Exemplar 21.B Pressure Injuries · RYB Wound Care & Debridement
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.stem: A client has a nonhealing Stage 4 pressure injury on the right heel with necrotic tissue and adequate arterial blood flow. The provider recommends biosurgery with sterile maggots. After teaching, which statement by the client indicates understanding?
options: “The maggots will eat into healthy tissue too, so I'll need a skin graft after.”
“The larvae digest dead tissue and do little harm to healthy tissue.”
“The maggots stay in place permanently until my wound has fully closed.”
“This treatment means I no longer have to keep pressure off my heel.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. Medical larvae digest necrotic tissue and cause minimal damage to healthy tissue.
Correct. Biosurgery uses sterile larvae to selectively digest necrotic tissue.
Incorrect. Larvae are applied in contained dressings for short cycles (commonly 2–4 days) and then removed; they are not permanent.
Incorrect. Offloading remains essential; debridement does not remove the cause of the injury.
questions.rationale: Biosurgery uses sterile maggots to digest dead tissue with minimal harm to healthy tissue. It treats the necrotic wound, but it does not remove the cause. Pressure relief (floating the heel) and nutrition support must continue, and the larvae are removed after treatment rather than left in place until the wound closes.
questions.takeaway: Maggots eat dead tissue, not healthy tissue — and heel offloading continues.
questions.hintContent: Recall how biosurgery works and that debridement does not replace prevention measures.
questions.hintStrategy: Check each statement for accuracy about the larvae AND about ongoing pressure relief.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Exemplar 21.B Pressure Injuries · RYB Wound Care & Debridement
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.stem: A nursing student is reviewing the debridement methods for a client whose pressure injury contains black necrotic tissue. Which pairings of method and debridement type are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Wet-to-dry dressing: mechanical debridement
Prescribed enzymes applied to necrotic tissue: autolytic debridement
Special dressing that captures drainage so the body's own enzymes break down dead tissue: autolytic debridement
Removal of eschar with a scalpel by a surgeon: sharp debridement
Wet-to-dry dressing: chemical debridement
optionRationales: Correct. A wet-to-dry dressing removes tissue mechanically when the dried gauze is pulled away.
Incorrect. Applying prescribed enzymes is chemical debridement.
Correct. Special dressings that let the body's own enzymes break down dead tissue provide autolytic debridement.
Correct. Removal with a scalpel by a surgeon is sharp debridement.
Incorrect. A wet-to-dry dressing is mechanical, not chemical, debridement.
questions.rationale: The slides list debridement as sharp (surgeon with a scalpel), mechanical (wet-to-dry dressing), chemical (enzymes), autolytic (special dressings that capture drainage), and biosurgery (sterile maggots). Nurses can debride within limits; sharp debridement is performed by the surgeon.
questions.takeaway: Wet-to-dry = mechanical; enzymes = chemical; special dressings = autolytic; scalpel = sharp.
questions.hintContent: Recall the five debridement methods on the slides and what each one uses.
questions.hintStrategy: For each pairing, ask what actually removes the dead tissue — force, applied enzymes, the body's own enzymes, or a blade.
